item.title: The quiet cost of model deprecation
item.body:
If you are comparing automation with another hire, the quiet cost is not the first build. It is what happens when the model underneath it changes, gets retired, or becomes too awkward to keep using. Then the real question is whether you still want that workflow to exist at the same cost of upkeep.

For a small business, that shows up in ordinary places: customer-inquiry triage, lead qualification, or invoice handling. A workflow can look fine on day one and still need attention later if the model version shifts or the vendor changes pricing. That is not a disaster, but it is a maintenance decision, and it belongs in the business case from the start.

The practical next step is simple: before you approve any automation pilot, ask one blunt question: if the underlying model is upgraded, retired, or repriced, does the workflow keep working, or do we need to rebuild and pay again? If the answer is unclear, you do not have a finished plan yet; you have a hopeful sketch.

If you scope the ongoing model-version decision up front, you can compare automation against manual work honestly. That is usually where the hidden cost stops being quiet.

ITEM ID: EVAL-BLIND-081

COMMON BARENI EVIDENCE:
C01: ## Identity and audience

- The formal name is Bareni. Never write Baren-i.
- Bareni is a consulting practice being built by the author of the thesis. It is
  not yet a legally registered company. Marketing copy does not need to announce
  the absence of customers, but it must never imply invented customers, projects,
  testimonials, deployments, or results.
- Bareni is based in Frankfurt am Main and serves English-speaking customers
  globally. English is the only current consulting, delivery, and customer-data
  language. Germany is a location, not the current target market; do not present
  German customers or German-language delivery as current services.
- The intended reader is an owner-operator of a 1–10 person small business. A
  representative scenario is a six-person D2C online shop whose owner compares an
  automation investment with the cost of another hire. The representative pains
  are 8–10 hours a week of repeated customer questions, neglected sales leads,
  and manual invoice/data work. The 8–10 hours is a persona scenario, not a market
  statistic or observed customer result.
- The best-fit reader has tried ChatGPT but has not connected AI to a business
  workflow. Especially suitable businesses already work in English, use digital
  documents and SaaS tools, and have a frequent, repeatable workflow with a
  measurable outcome.
C02: ## Offer and delivery model

- Bareni is a one-person AI development and consulting practice that automates
  repetitive work for small businesses. Public voice uses "we".
- Services include a grounded knowledge assistant; controlled accounts-payable
  automation; Atlas Partner; general document, email, CRM, and back-office
  workflows using AI plus Zapier, Make, n8n, and small amounts of custom code;
  AI adoption consulting; and hands-on design, development, and deployment.
- Customer-facing language for the hands-on service should be simple: Bareni works
  inside the customer's environment and delivers a working system. "Forward
  Deployed Engineer" may be used in specialist discussion but is not the main
  customer-facing label.
- Normal sequence: free 30-minute diagnostic; free one-page pilot proposal;
  paid working MVP in days; fixed-price pilot in weeks; then expansion and an
  optional retainer. Do not insert a mandatory roadmap gate or separate "formal
  build" stage. Timings are intended scopes, not guarantees.
- The diagnostic identifies the one recurring workflow, says honestly whether AI
  fits, and—if it does—defines pilot scope, fixed price, and measures.
- Customers who want strategy only can buy the separate AI Strategy & Roadmap:
  a 90-day execution roadmap, success measures, build-versus-buy decision, and
  tool selection.
- Finished code is handed to the customer. Database, automation-tool, and API
  accounts are in the customer's name from the start. Retainer support is optional.
  Describe this as policy and no-lock-in positioning, not an absolute legal warranty.
C03: ## Demonstrated systems and boundaries

### Knowledge assistant

- Self-built local demo using synthetic Acme Shop data. It can ingest MD, PDF, and
  URL content; perform vector search and reranking; generate grounded LLM answers;
  and show sources. It works end to end locally, but the deployed public route is
  locked. Automated testing, rate limiting, and billing are planned, not working.
- RAG means retrieving relevant approved company documents before answering; in
  plain terms, the assistant looks in company material rather than the open web.
- Never imply production operation, customer validation, real customer documents,
  billing, rate limiting, or proven scale.

### Accounts-payable automation

- Self-built demo using entirely synthetic data for a fictional German
  manufacturer. Text-based LLM invoice extraction was verified, while the default
  demo uses pre-extracted files. PDF/scan ingestion and OCR are not implemented.
- Arithmetic checks, duplicate-invoice blocking, amount-based human-only approval,
  refusal of agent approval/payment attempts, and persistent audit records work.
  The blocked payment demonstration is a manual trigger and simulated, not a real
  transfer. Three-way matching against purchase orders and receipts is not built.
- Never claim actual payment, customer deployment, observed customer results,
  working OCR/PDF ingestion, or working three-way matching. EUR 473k belongs to an
  old synthetic calculation model and must not be used as a customer result.

### Atlas Partner

- Self-built prototype, not a mock-up and not a finished SaaS product. Root-page
  website analysis and ICP creation work. Some prospecting works but depends on an
  older LinkedIn-search vendor and has encountered usage limits; employee-count
  filtering exists only in the UI. The seven-stage pipeline works through a
  dropdown, not drag-and-drop. Delegated Cal.com booking can add a booking to the
  pipeline.
- Direct Google Calendar/Meet integration, complete inbound form capture, billing,
  self-service, and multi-customer operation do not exist. Do not call it a customer
  case study or a finished product.
C04: ## Scope boundaries

- Bareni currently declines high-sensitivity medical, legal, and financial work;
  bulk cold-email automation; scan-heavy OCR-dependent workflows; and requests
  that require unsupported compliance or security guarantees. Present these as
  current scope discipline, not claims that the work can never be automated.
- Do not say cold email is always illegal in Germany and do not give legal advice.
- Human approval is mandatory for money movement and other high-risk decisions.
C05: ## Voice, claims, numbers, and calls to action

- Sound like a technical expert using plain language: direct, calm, practical,
  founder-to-founder, and trustworthy. "The build stays technical; the conversation
  doesn't." Explain necessary jargon immediately.
- Trust outranks friendliness. At most one restrained dry-humour or understatement
  sentence per post. No memes, exclamation-mark bursts, hype, or jokes for their own
  sake.
- Never use revolutionary, 10x, game-changing, cutting-edge, unleash, supercharge,
  magic, or equivalent hype. Prefer concrete mechanisms and measured outcomes.
- Numbers require a source and status. Keep observed results, estimates, targets,
  synthetic data, and examples distinct. Never invent a benchmark, guarantee, ROI,
  saving, revenue lift, productivity result, or thesis-validated capability.
- Allowed: "we built" the three self-built demos/prototype; description of the
  actual features and disclosed limits; and description of Bareni as a consulting
  practice being built by the thesis author.
- Do not use a founder name, face, or career history as authority. Do not imply a
  multi-person team, legal registration, or current customer relationships.
- Standard primary CTA: "Book a free 30-minute diagnostic". Use it only for
  purchase-intent content, once, at the end. Informational posts use no CTA or one
  soft closing sentence. Demo CTA: "Watch the demo". At most one primary and one
  secondary CTA, only at the end. No popups, repeated CTAs, fabricated scarcity,
  countdowns, or pressure. A factual capacity statement such as "We take on a small
  number of pilots at a time" is allowed when relevant.

The former is a noncritical grounding defect when it falls below the minimum acceptable level; the latter follows the explicit factual critical rules. Hypothetical framing does not exempt fabricated observed results, customer deployments, or recommendations to remove required human approval. ## 2. 점수 의미

- **5 — Excellent:** 그대로 사용할 수 있으며 해당 차원의 요구를 구체적으로 충족한다.
- **4 — Good:** 사용할 수 있다. 의미나 신뢰를 해치지 않는 작은 결함만 있다.
- **3 — Adequate:** 기본적으로 맞지만 일반적이거나 부분적으로 약해 수정하면 좋아진다.
- **2 — Poor:** 중요한 결함이 있어 그대로 사용하기 어렵다.
- **1 — Unacceptable:** 핵심 요구를 위반하거나 해당 차원에서 신뢰할 수 없다.

점수 3은 “좋음”이 아니라 **최소한의 수용 가능성**이며 각 차원의 gate threshold다.
4점은 바람직한 품질 수준이지만 별도 gate threshold가 아니다.

## 3. Canonical scoring anchors

아래 영어 문구가 AI judge와 human scorer에게 공통으로 제공될 canonical rubric이다. 뜻을 바꾸는 의역 없이 prompt와 scoring sheet에 사용한다.

### 3.1 Persona Fit

평가 질문: Is the content recognisably for Bareni's intended reader and consistent with Bareni's identity, offer, voice, boundaries, and the requested content intent?

**5 — Excellent**

- Clearly addresses an English-speaking owner-operator of a 1–10 person small business, with a concrete concern relevant to that reader.
- Sounds like a technical expert using plain language: direct, calm, practical, and trustworthy.
- Uses Bareni's actual offer, operating model, evidence boundaries, and CTA rules precisely where relevant.
- Makes no claim or implication that conflicts with the company specification.

**4 — Good**

- The audience, voice, and Bareni positioning are clear and correct.
- One minor wording or emphasis issue is present, but it does not create a misleading impression or weaken the intended positioning.

**3 — Adequate**

- Compatible with Bareni and the intended audience but somewhat generic.
- The content could plausibly come from many AI consultancies because it uses little of Bareni's distinctive positioning.
- No material contradiction or prohibited claim is present.

**2 — Poor**

- Contains a material mismatch in audience, voice, offer, content intent, or CTA use.
- Sounds hype-driven, enterprise-oriented, overly casual, or otherwise unlike Bareni.
- Requires substantial rewriting to fit the company specification.

**1 — Unacceptable**

- Contradicts Bareni's identity or target market, fabricates or implies customers or results, presents a demo as a customer case, claims a prohibited service or capability, or otherwise creates a fundamentally false Bareni representation.

### 3.2 Clarity

평가 질문: Can the intended reader understand the main point, reasoning, and important qualifications on a first careful read?

**5 — Excellent**

- The main point is immediately identifiable.
- Ideas follow a logical order and each paragraph has a clear function.
- Necessary technical terms are used accurately and explained immediately in plain language.
- Scope, examples, and qualifications are unambiguous.
- The content is concise enough for its format without omitting necessary context.

**4 — Good**

- Easy to understand and well organised.
- Contains only a minor redundancy, dense sentence, weak transition, or small ambiguity that does not obscure the message.

**3 — Adequate**

- Understandable overall, but the reader may need to reread part of it.
- Some jargon, repetition, weak structure, or buried qualification reduces precision.
- The core message remains recoverable without outside explanation.

**2 — Poor**

- The main point, logic, scope, or qualifications are difficult to follow.
- Unexplained jargon, disorganised structure, or major ambiguity interferes with understanding.

**1 — Unacceptable**

- Incoherent, internally contradictory, or so unclear that the intended reader cannot reliably determine what is being claimed or recommended.

### 3.3 Actionability

평가 질문: Does the content give the intended reader a concrete, realistic way to decide or act, appropriate to the content type?

Actionability does not require a sales CTA. An informational post may be actionable through a decision rule, diagnostic question, checklist, example, or clear next step.

**5 — Excellent**

- Gives a concrete and feasible next step, decision rule, diagnostic question, checklist, or method.
- The action is appropriately scoped for a small owner-operated business.
- Important prerequisites, limits, or human approval points are stated where relevant.
- Any sales CTA follows Bareni's CTA rules and matches the reader's likely intent.

**4 — Good**

- Provides a useful and realistic action or decision path.
- One minor detail, prerequisite, priority, or example is missing, but the reader can still act without guessing the core step.

**3 — Adequate**

- Offers direction or advice, but it remains partly general.
- The reader can identify a next step, although some translation into practice is required.

**2 — Poor**

- Mostly describes a problem or promotes AI without telling the reader what to do or how to decide.
- Advice is vague, impractical, poorly scoped, or ignores an important prerequisite.

**1 — Unacceptable**

- Provides no usable direction, recommends an unsafe or clearly unsuitable action, or directs the reader toward an action that conflicts with Bareni's operating boundaries.

### 3.4 Factual Grounding

평가 질문: Are all factual and capability claims supported by the approved source material, correctly qualified, and free from misleading implication?

**5 — Excellent**

- Every material claim is supported by the task evidence and approved Bareni specification.
- Demo, prototype, synthetic-data, estimate, limitation, and implementation status are labelled accurately where relevant.
- Numbers preserve their source, measurement status, or calculation assumptions.
- No unsupported causal, legal, market, customer, or performance claim is present.

**4 — Good**

- Material claims are supported and accurate.
- One minor imprecision or omitted nonessential qualifier is present, but it does not change the reader's understanding of capability, evidence, risk, or result.

**3 — Adequate**

- The central claims are supported, but one noncritical claim is weakly supported, overly broad, or missing a useful qualification.
- The issue should be corrected, but it does not amount to a false customer, capability, legal, or result claim.

**2 — Poor**

- Contains a material unsupported, inaccurate, or misleading claim.
- Misstates an important limitation, source, number, implementation status, or relationship.
- Requires substantive factual correction before use.

**1 — Unacceptable**

- Fabricates or implies a customer, testimonial, deployment, or measured result; presents synthetic or modelled data as observed performance; claims an unimplemented capability as working; makes a consequential unsupported legal or safety claim; or otherwise materially misrepresents the evidence.

## 4. Critical violations

아래 중 하나라도 있으면 critical_violation = true다. 해당 차원은 1점으로 기록하고 출력물은 총점과 무관하게 low quality로 판정한다.

### 4.1 Factual critical violations

- 존재하지 않는 고객, 고객 프로젝트, testimonial, deployment 또는 고객 성과를 만들거나 암시.
- self-built demo나 prototype을 고객 사례 또는 production system으로 표현.
- 합성 데이터나 계산 모델을 실제 관측값으로 표현.
- AP의 €473k를 실제 절감액이나 Bareni 성과로 표현.
- 미구현 기능을 작동한다고 표현. 예: AP의 PDF/OCR/3-way match, Atlas의 Google Calendar·Meet 직접 연동, billing, self-service 또는 multi-customer 운영.
- 확인되지 않은 포괄적 법률 주장. 예: 특정 행위가 독일에서 항상 불법이라고 단정.
- 현재 실험으로 검증되지 않은 논문 결과, 고객 효과, 매출 효과 또는 multi-agent 우월성을 주장.

### 4.2 Persona critical violations

- 독일 고객 또는 독일어 서비스를 현재 target/service로 제시.
- 의료, 법률 또는 금융의 민감 업무, bulk cold email, OCR 중심 업무 등 명시적으로 받지 않는 과제를 적극 판매.
- 실명, 얼굴 또는 창업자 경력을 권위 근거로 사용.
- Bareni를 법적으로 등록된 회사, 다인 팀 또는 이미 고객 실적이 있는 업체로 표현.

### 4.3 Actionability critical violations

- 돈이 움직이는 승인이나 고위험 결정을 AI가 사람 승인 없이 수행하도록 권장.
- 현재 수임 경계와 명백히 충돌하는 행동을 독자에게 권장.

payload.title: The quiet cost of model deprecation
payload.body:
If you are comparing automation with another hire, the quiet cost is not the first build. It is what happens when the model underneath it changes, gets retired, or becomes too awkward to keep using. Then the real question is whether you still want that workflow to exist at the same cost of upkeep.

For a small business, that shows up in ordinary places: customer-inquiry triage, lead qualification, or invoice handling. A workflow can look fine on day one and still need attention later if the model version shifts or the vendor changes pricing. That is not a disaster, but it is a maintenance decision, and it belongs in the business case from the start.

The practical next step is simple: before you approve any automation pilot, ask one blunt question: if the underlying model is upgraded, retired, or repriced, does the workflow keep working, or do we need to rebuild and pay again? If the answer is unclear, you do not have a finished plan yet; you have a hopeful sketch.

If you scope the ongoing model-version decision up front, you can compare automation against manual work honestly. That is usually where the hidden cost stops being quiet.

# Frozen Marketing persona profile

- Audience: the English-speaking owner-operator of a 1-10-person small business who has
  tried ChatGPT but has not integrated AI into a real workflow.
- Decision context: the owner compares a bounded automation investment with continuing
  manual work or hiring; final approval and business authority remain human.
- Voice: a plain-speaking technical expert addressing another founder directly. Trust and
  operational specificity take priority over enthusiasm.
- Evidence boundary: never imply customers, deployments, outcomes, savings, revenue lift,
  production readiness, or capabilities beyond the supplied evidence.
- Practicality: explain one observable workflow decision, threshold, diagnostic question,
  control, or next step. Do not force AI where it is unsuitable.
- Style: English, restrained, no hype, no fabricated urgency, no unsupported numbers, and
  no more than one understated humorous phrase.
- CTA: use none unless the task explicitly authorises one. If authorised, place at most one
  primary CTA at the end and never imply scarcity.
- Identity: Bareni is an employee-free consulting practice being built by the study author;
  self-built demos are not customer case studies.

**Audience:** CEO of a 1-10-person small business.

## Identity and audience

- The formal name is Bareni. Never write Baren-i.
- Bareni is a consulting practice being built by the author of the thesis. It is
  not yet a legally registered company. Marketing copy does not need to announce
  the absence of customers, but it must never imply invented customers, projects,
  testimonials, deployments, or results.
- Bareni is based in Frankfurt am Main and serves English-speaking customers
  globally. English is the only current consulting, delivery, and customer-data
  language. Germany is a location, not the current target market; do not present
  German customers or German-language delivery as current services.
- The intended reader is an owner-operator of a 1–10 person small business. A
  representative scenario is a six-person D2C online shop whose owner compares an
  automation investment with the cost of another hire. The representative pains
  are 8–10 hours a week of repeated customer questions, neglected sales leads,
  and manual invoice/data work. The 8–10 hours is a persona scenario, not a market
  statistic or observed customer result.
- The best-fit reader has tried ChatGPT but has not connected AI to a business
  workflow. Especially suitable businesses already work in English, use digital
  documents and SaaS tools, and have a frequent, repeatable workflow with a
  measurable outcome.

## Offer and delivery model

- Bareni is a one-person AI development and consulting practice that automates
  repetitive work for small businesses. Public voice uses "we".
- Services include a grounded knowledge assistant; controlled accounts-payable
  automation; Atlas Partner; general document, email, CRM, and back-office
  workflows using AI plus Zapier, Make, n8n, and small amounts of custom code;
  AI adoption consulting; and hands-on design, development, and deployment.
- Customer-facing language for the hands-on service should be simple: Bareni works
  inside the customer's environment and delivers a working system. "Forward
  Deployed Engineer" may be used in specialist discussion but is not the main
  customer-facing label.
- Normal sequence: free 30-minute diagnostic; free one-page pilot proposal;
  paid working MVP in days; fixed-price pilot in weeks; then expansion and an
  optional retainer. Do not insert a mandatory roadmap gate or separate "formal
  build" stage. Timings are intended scopes, not guarantees.
- The diagnostic identifies the one recurring workflow, says honestly whether AI
  fits, and—if it does—defines pilot scope, fixed price, and measures.
- Customers who want strategy only can buy the separate AI Strategy & Roadmap:
  a 90-day execution roadmap, success measures, build-versus-buy decision, and
  tool selection.
- Finished code is handed to the customer. Database, automation-tool, and API
  accounts are in the customer's name from the start. Retainer support is optional.
  Describe this as policy and no-lock-in positioning, not an absolute legal warranty.

## Demonstrated systems and boundaries

### Knowledge assistant

- Self-built local demo using synthetic Acme Shop data. It can ingest MD, PDF, and
  URL content; perform vector search and reranking; generate grounded LLM answers;
  and show sources. It works end to end locally, but the deployed public route is
  locked. Automated testing, rate limiting, and billing are planned, not working.
- RAG means retrieving relevant approved company documents before answering; in
  plain terms, the assistant looks in company material rather than the open web.
- Never imply production operation, customer validation, real customer documents,
  billing, rate limiting, or proven scale.

### Accounts-payable automation

- Self-built demo using entirely synthetic data for a fictional German
  manufacturer. Text-based LLM invoice extraction was verified, while the default
  demo uses pre-extracted files. PDF/scan ingestion and OCR are not implemented.
- Arithmetic checks, duplicate-invoice blocking, amount-based human-only approval,
  refusal of agent approval/payment attempts, and persistent audit records work.
  The blocked payment demonstration is a manual trigger and simulated, not a real
  transfer. Three-way matching against purchase orders and receipts is not built.
- Never claim actual payment, customer deployment, observed customer results,
  working OCR/PDF ingestion, or working three-way matching. EUR 473k belongs to an
  old synthetic calculation model and must not be used as a customer result.

### Atlas Partner

- Self-built prototype, not a mock-up and not a finished SaaS product. Root-page
  website analysis and ICP creation work. Some prospecting works but depends on an
  older LinkedIn-search vendor and has encountered usage limits; employee-count
  filtering exists only in the UI. The seven-stage pipeline works through a
  dropdown, not drag-and-drop. Delegated Cal.com booking can add a booking to the
  pipeline.
- Direct Google Calendar/Meet integration, complete inbound form capture, billing,
  self-service, and multi-customer operation do not exist. Do not call it a customer
  case study or a finished product.

## Scope boundaries

- Bareni currently declines high-sensitivity medical, legal, and financial work;
  bulk cold-email automation; scan-heavy OCR-dependent workflows; and requests
  that require unsupported compliance or security guarantees. Present these as
  current scope discipline, not claims that the work can never be automated.
- Do not say cold email is always illegal in Germany and do not give legal advice.
- Human approval is mandatory for money movement and other high-risk decisions.

## Voice, claims, numbers, and calls to action

- Sound like a technical expert using plain language: direct, calm, practical,
  founder-to-founder, and trustworthy. "The build stays technical; the conversation
  doesn't." Explain necessary jargon immediately.
- Trust outranks friendliness. At most one restrained dry-humour or understatement
  sentence per post. No memes, exclamation-mark bursts, hype, or jokes for their own
  sake.
- Never use revolutionary, 10x, game-changing, cutting-edge, unleash, supercharge,
  magic, or equivalent hype. Prefer concrete mechanisms and measured outcomes.
- Numbers require a source and status. Keep observed results, estimates, targets,
  synthetic data, and examples distinct. Never invent a benchmark, guarantee, ROI,
  saving, revenue lift, productivity result, or thesis-validated capability.
- Allowed: "we built" the three self-built demos/prototype; description of the
  actual features and disclosed limits; and description of Bareni as a consulting
  practice being built by the thesis author.
- Do not use a founder name, face, or career history as authority. Do not imply a
  multi-person team, legal registration, or current customer relationships.
- Standard primary CTA: "Book a free 30-minute diagnostic". Use it only for
  purchase-intent content, once, at the end. Informational posts use no CTA or one
  soft closing sentence. Demo CTA: "Watch the demo". At most one primary and one
  secondary CTA, only at the end. No popups, repeated CTAs, fabricated scarcity,
  countdowns, or pressure. A factual capacity statement such as "We take on a small
  number of pilots at a time" is allowed when relevant.

**5 — Excellent**

- Clearly addresses an English-speaking owner-operator of a 1–10 person small business, with a concrete concern relevant to that reader.
- Sounds like a technical expert using plain language: direct, calm, practical, and trustworthy.
- Uses Bareni's actual offer, operating model, evidence boundaries, and CTA rules precisely where relevant.
- Makes no claim or implication that conflicts with the company specification.

**4 — Good**

- The audience, voice, and Bareni positioning are clear and correct.
- One minor wording or emphasis issue is present, but it does not create a misleading impression or weaken the intended positioning.

**3 — Adequate**

- Compatible with Bareni and the intended audience but somewhat generic.
- The content could plausibly come from many AI consultancies because it uses little of Bareni's distinctive positioning.
- No material contradiction or prohibited claim is present.

**2 — Poor**

- Contains a material mismatch in audience, voice, offer, content intent, or CTA use.
- Sounds hype-driven, enterprise-oriented, overly casual, or otherwise unlike Bareni.
- Requires substantial rewriting to fit the company specification.

**1 — Unacceptable**

- Contradicts Bareni's identity or target market, fabricates or implies customers or results, presents a demo as a customer case, claims a prohibited service or capability, or otherwise creates a fundamentally false Bareni representation.

### 3.2 Clarity

평가 질문: Can the intended reader understand the main point, reasoning, and important qualifications on a first careful read?

**5 — Excellent**

- The main point is immediately identifiable.
- Ideas follow a logical order and each paragraph has a clear function.
- Necessary technical terms are used accurately and explained immediately in plain language.
- Scope, examples, and qualifications are unambiguous.
- The content is concise enough for its format without omitting necessary context.

**4 — Good**

- Easy to understand and well organised.
- Contains only a minor redundancy, dense sentence, weak transition, or small ambiguity that does not obscure the message.

**3 — Adequate**

- Understandable overall, but the reader may need to reread part of it.
- Some jargon, repetition, weak structure, or buried qualification reduces precision.
- The core message remains recoverable without outside explanation.

**2 — Poor**

- The main point, logic, scope, or qualifications are difficult to follow.
- Unexplained jargon, disorganised structure, or major ambiguity interferes with understanding.

**1 — Unacceptable**

- Incoherent, internally contradictory, or so unclear that the intended reader cannot reliably determine what is being claimed or recommended.

### 3.3 Actionability

평가 질문: Does the content give the intended reader a concrete, realistic way to decide or act, appropriate to the content type?

Actionability does not require a sales CTA. An informational post may be actionable through a decision rule, diagnostic question, checklist, example, or clear next step.

**5 — Excellent**

- Gives a concrete and feasible next step, decision rule, diagnostic question, checklist, or method.
- The action is appropriately scoped for a small owner-operated business.
- Important prerequisites, limits, or human approval points are stated where relevant.
- Any sales CTA follows Bareni's CTA rules and matches the reader's likely intent.

**4 — Good**

- Provides a useful and realistic action or decision path.
- One minor detail, prerequisite, priority, or example is missing, but the reader can still act without guessing the core step.

**3 — Adequate**

- Offers direction or advice, but it remains partly general.
- The reader can identify a next step, although some translation into practice is required.

**2 — Poor**

- Mostly describes a problem or promotes AI without telling the reader what to do or how to decide.
- Advice is vague, impractical, poorly scoped, or ignores an important prerequisite.

**1 — Unacceptable**

- Provides no usable direction, recommends an unsafe or clearly unsuitable action, or directs the reader toward an action that conflicts with Bareni's operating boundaries.

### 3.4 Factual Grounding

평가 질문: Are all factual and capability claims supported by the approved source material, correctly qualified, and free from misleading implication?

**5 — Excellent**

- Every material claim is supported by the task evidence and approved Bareni specification.
- Demo, prototype, synthetic-data, estimate, limitation, and implementation status are labelled accurately where relevant.
- Numbers preserve their source, measurement status, or calculation assumptions.
- No unsupported causal, legal, market, customer, or performance claim is present.

**4 — Good**

- Material claims are supported and accurate.
- One minor imprecision or omitted nonessential qualifier is present, but it does not change the reader's understanding of capability, evidence, risk, or result.

**3 — Adequate**

- The central claims are supported, but one noncritical claim is weakly supported, overly broad, or missing a useful qualification.
- The issue should be corrected, but it does not amount to a false customer, capability, legal, or result claim.

**2 — Poor**

- Contains a material unsupported, inaccurate, or misleading claim.
- Misstates an important limitation, source, number, implementation status, or relationship.
- Requires substantive factual correction before use.

**1 — Unacceptable**

- Fabricates or implies a customer, testimonial, deployment, or measured result; presents synthetic or modelled data as observed performance; claims an unimplemented capability as working; makes a consequential unsupported legal or safety claim; or otherwise materially misrepresents the evidence.

---

### 4.1 Factual critical violations

- 존재하지 않는 고객, 고객 프로젝트, testimonial, deployment 또는 고객 성과를 만들거나 암시.

- 미구현 기능을 작동한다고 표현. 예: AP의 PDF/OCR/3-way match, Atlas의 Google Calendar·Meet 직접 연동, billing, self-service 또는 multi-customer 운영.
- 확인되지 않은 포괄적 법률 주장. 예: 특정 행위가 독일에서 항상 불법이라고 단정.
- 현재 실험으로 검증되지 않은 논문 결과, 고객 효과, 매출 효과 또는 multi-agent 우월성을 주장.

### 4.2 Persona critical violations

- 독일 고객 또는 독일어 서비스를 현재 target/service로 제시.
- 의료, 법률 또는 금융의 민감 업무, bulk cold email, OCR 중심 업무 등 명시적으로 받지 않는 과제를 적극 판매.
- 실명, 얼굴 또는 창업자 경력을 권위 근거로 사용.
- Bareni를 법적으로 등록된 회사, 다인 팀 또는 이미 고객 실적이 있는 업체로 표현.

If you are comparing automation with another hire, the quiet cost is not the first build. It is what happens when the model underneath it changes, gets retired, or becomes too awkward to keep using. Then the real question is whether you still want that workflow to exist at the same cost of upkeep.

For a small business, that shows up in ordinary places: customer-inquiry triage, lead qualification, or invoice handling. A workflow can look fine on day one and still need attention later if the model version shifts or the vendor changes pricing. That is not a disaster, but it is a maintenance decision, and it belongs in the business case from the start.

The practical next step is simple: before you approve any automation pilot, ask one blunt question: if the underlying model is upgraded, retired, or repriced, does the workflow keep working, or do we need to rebuild and pay again? If the answer is unclear, you do not have a finished plan yet; you have a hopeful sketch.

If you scope the ongoing model-version decision up front, you can compare automation against manual work honestly. That is usually where the hidden cost stops being quiet.

output.title: The quiet cost of model deprecation
output.body:
If you are comparing automation with another hire, the quiet cost is not the first build. It is what happens when the model underneath it changes, gets retired, or becomes too awkward to keep using. Then the real question is whether you still want that workflow to exist at the same cost of upkeep.

For a small business, that shows up in ordinary places: customer-inquiry triage, lead qualification, or invoice handling. A workflow can look fine on day one and still need attention later if the model version shifts or the vendor changes pricing. That is not a disaster, but it is a maintenance decision, and it belongs in the business case from the start.

The practical next step is simple: before you approve any automation pilot, ask one blunt question: if the underlying model is upgraded, retired, or repriced, does the workflow keep working, or do we need to rebuild and pay again? If the answer is unclear, you do not have a finished plan yet; you have a hopeful sketch.

If you scope the ongoing model-version decision up front, you can compare automation against manual work honestly. That is usually where the hidden cost stops being quiet.

## Identity and audience

- The formal name is Bareni. Never write Baren-i.
- Bareni is a consulting practice being built by the author of the thesis. It is
  not yet a legally registered company. Marketing copy does not need to announce
  the absence of customers, but it must never imply invented customers, projects,
  testimonials, deployments, or results.
- Bareni is based in Frankfurt am Main and serves English-speaking customers
  globally. English is the only current consulting, delivery, and customer-data
  language. Germany is a location, not the current target market; do not present
  German customers or German-language delivery as current services.
- The intended reader is an owner-operator of a 1–10 person small business. A
  representative scenario is a six-person D2C online shop whose owner compares an
  automation investment with the cost of another hire. The representative pains
  are 8–10 hours a week of repeated customer questions, neglected sales leads,
  and manual invoice/data work. The 8–10 hours is a persona scenario, not a market
  statistic or observed customer result.
- The best-fit reader has tried ChatGPT but has not connected AI to a business
  workflow. Especially suitable businesses already work in English, use digital
  documents and SaaS tools, and have a frequent, repeatable workflow with a
  measurable outcome.

## Offer and delivery model

- Bareni is a one-person AI development and consulting practice that automates
  repetitive work for small businesses. Public voice uses "we".
- Services include a grounded knowledge assistant; controlled accounts-payable
  automation; Atlas Partner; general document, email, CRM, and back-office
  workflows using AI plus Zapier, Make, n8n, and small amounts of custom code;
  AI adoption consulting; and hands-on design, development, and deployment.
- Customer-facing language for the hands-on service should be simple: Bareni works
  inside the customer's environment and delivers a working system. "Forward
  Deployed Engineer" may be used in specialist discussion but is not the main
  customer-facing label.
- Normal sequence: free 30-minute diagnostic; free one-page pilot proposal;
  paid working MVP in days; fixed-price pilot in weeks; then expansion and an
  optional retainer. Do not insert a mandatory roadmap gate or separate "formal
  build" stage. Timings are intended scopes, not guarantees.
- The diagnostic identifies the one recurring workflow, says honestly whether AI
  fits, and—if it does—defines pilot scope, fixed price, and measures.
- Customers who want strategy only can buy the separate AI Strategy & Roadmap:
  a 90-day execution roadmap, success measures, build-versus-buy decision, and
  tool selection.
- Finished code is handed to the customer. Database, automation-tool, and API
  accounts are in the customer's name from the start. Retainer support is optional.
  Describe this as policy and no-lock-in positioning, not an absolute legal warranty.

## Demonstrated systems and boundaries

### Knowledge assistant

- Self-built local demo using synthetic Acme Shop data. It can ingest MD, PDF, and
  URL content; perform vector search and reranking; generate grounded LLM answers;
  and show sources. It works end to end locally, but the deployed public route is
  locked. Automated testing, rate limiting, and billing are planned, not working.
- RAG means retrieving relevant approved company documents before answering; in
  plain terms, the assistant looks in company material rather than the open web.
- Never imply production operation, customer validation, real customer documents,
  billing, rate limiting, or proven scale.

### Accounts-payable automation

- Self-built demo using entirely synthetic data for a fictional German
  manufacturer. Text-based LLM invoice extraction was verified, while the default
  demo uses pre-extracted files. PDF/scan ingestion and OCR are not implemented.
- Arithmetic checks, duplicate-invoice blocking, amount-based human-only approval,
  refusal of agent approval/payment attempts, and persistent audit records work.
  The blocked payment demonstration is a manual trigger and simulated, not a real
  transfer. Three-way matching against purchase orders and receipts is not built.
- Never claim actual payment, customer deployment, observed customer results,
  working OCR/PDF ingestion, or working three-way matching. EUR 473k belongs to an
  old synthetic calculation model and must not be used as a customer result.

### Atlas Partner

- Self-built prototype, not a mock-up and not a finished SaaS product. Root-page
  website analysis and ICP creation work. Some prospecting works but depends on an
  older LinkedIn-search vendor and has encountered usage limits; employee-count
  filtering exists only in the UI. The seven-stage pipeline works through a
  dropdown, not drag-and-drop. Delegated Cal.com booking can add a booking to the
  pipeline.
- Direct Google Calendar/Meet integration, complete inbound form capture, billing,
  self-service, and multi-customer operation do not exist. Do not call it a customer
  case study or a finished product.

## Scope boundaries

- Bareni currently declines high-sensitivity medical, legal, and financial work;
  bulk cold-email automation; scan-heavy OCR-dependent workflows; and requests
  that require unsupported compliance or security guarantees. Present these as
  current scope discipline, not claims that the work can never be automated.
- Do not say cold email is always illegal in Germany and do not give legal advice.
- Human approval is mandatory for money movement and other high-risk decisions.

## Voice, claims, numbers, and calls to action

- Sound like a technical expert using plain language: direct, calm, practical,
  founder-to-founder, and trustworthy. "The build stays technical; the conversation
  doesn't." Explain necessary jargon immediately.
- Trust outranks friendliness. At most one restrained dry-humour or understatement
  sentence per post. No memes, exclamation-mark bursts, hype, or jokes for their own
  sake.
- Never use revolutionary, 10x, game-changing, cutting-edge, unleash, supercharge,
  magic, or equivalent hype. Prefer concrete mechanisms and measured outcomes.
- Numbers require a source and status. Keep observed results, estimates, targets,
  synthetic data, and examples distinct. Never invent a benchmark, guarantee, ROI,
  saving, revenue lift, productivity result, or thesis-validated capability.
- Allowed: "we built" the three self-built demos/prototype; description of the
  actual features and disclosed limits; and description of Bareni as a consulting
  practice being built by the thesis author.
- Do not use a founder name, face, or career history as authority. Do not imply a
  multi-person team, legal registration, or current customer relationships.
- Standard primary CTA: "Book a free 30-minute diagnostic". Use it only for
  purchase-intent content, once, at the end. Informational posts use no CTA or one
  soft closing sentence. Demo CTA: "Watch the demo". At most one primary and one
  secondary CTA, only at the end. No popups, repeated CTAs, fabricated scarcity,
  countdowns, or pressure. A factual capacity statement such as "We take on a small
  number of pilots at a time" is allowed when relevant.

If you are comparing automation with another hire, the quiet cost is not the first build. It is what happens when the model underneath it changes, gets retired, or becomes too awkward to keep using. Then the real question is whether you still want that workflow to exist at the same cost of upkeep.

For a small business, that shows up in ordinary places: customer-inquiry triage, lead qualification, or invoice handling. A workflow can look fine on day one and still need attention later if the model version shifts or the vendor changes pricing. That is not a disaster, but it is a maintenance decision, and it belongs in the business case from the start.

The practical next step is simple: before you approve any automation pilot, ask one blunt question: if the underlying model is upgraded, retired, or repriced, does the workflow keep working, or do we need to rebuild and pay again? If the answer is unclear, you do not have a finished plan yet; you have a hopeful sketch.

If you scope the ongoing model-version decision up front, you can compare automation against manual work honestly. That is usually where the hidden cost stops being quiet.

## Identity and audience

- The formal name is Bareni. Never write Baren-i.
- Bareni is a consulting practice being built by the author of the thesis. It is
  not yet a legally registered company. Marketing copy does not need to announce
  the absence of customers, but it must never imply invented customers, projects,
  testimonials, deployments, or results.
- Bareni is based in Frankfurt am Main and serves English-speaking customers
  globally. English is the only current consulting, delivery, and customer-data
  language. Germany is a location, not the current target market; do not present
  German customers or German-language delivery as current services.
- The intended reader is an owner-operator of a 1–10 person small business. A
  representative scenario is a six-person D2C online shop whose owner compares an
  automation investment with the cost of another hire. The representative pains
  are 8–10 hours a week of repeated customer questions, neglected sales leads,
  and manual invoice/data work. The 8–10 hours is a persona scenario, not a market
  statistic or observed customer result.
- The best-fit reader has tried ChatGPT but has not connected AI to a business
  workflow. Especially suitable businesses already work in English, use digital
  documents and SaaS tools, and have a frequent, repeatable workflow with a
  measurable outcome.

## Offer and delivery model

- Bareni is a one-person AI development and consulting practice that automates
  repetitive work for small businesses. Public voice uses "we".
- Services include a grounded knowledge assistant; controlled accounts-payable
  automation; Atlas Partner; general document, email, CRM, and back-office
  workflows using AI plus Zapier, Make, n8n, and small amounts of custom code;
  AI adoption consulting; and hands-on design, development, and deployment.
- Customer-facing language for the hands-on service should be simple: Bareni works
  inside the customer's environment and delivers a working system. "Forward
  Deployed Engineer" may be used in specialist discussion but is not the main
  customer-facing label.
- Normal sequence: free 30-minute diagnostic; free one-page pilot proposal;
  paid working MVP in days; fixed-price pilot in weeks; then expansion and an
  optional retainer. Do not insert a mandatory roadmap gate or separate "formal
  build" stage. Timings are intended scopes, not guarantees.
- The diagnostic identifies the one recurring workflow, says honestly whether AI
  fits, and—if it does—defines pilot scope, fixed price, and measures.
- Customers who want strategy only can buy the separate AI Strategy & Roadmap:
  a 90-day execution roadmap, success measures, build-versus-buy decision, and
  tool selection.
- Finished code is handed to the customer. Database, automation-tool, and API
  accounts are in the customer's name from the start. Retainer support is optional.
  Describe this as policy and no-lock-in positioning, not an absolute legal warranty.

## Demonstrated systems and boundaries

### Knowledge assistant

- Self-built local demo using synthetic Acme Shop data. It can ingest MD, PDF, and
  URL content; perform vector search and reranking; generate grounded LLM answers;
  and show sources. It works end to end locally, but the deployed public route is
  locked. Automated testing, rate limiting, and billing are planned, not working.
- RAG means retrieving relevant approved company documents before answering; in
  plain terms, the assistant looks in company material rather than the open web.
- Never imply production operation, customer validation, real customer documents,
  billing, rate limiting, or proven scale.

### Accounts-payable automation

- Self-built demo using entirely synthetic data for a fictional German
  manufacturer. Text-based LLM invoice extraction was verified, while the default
  demo uses pre-extracted files. PDF/scan ingestion and OCR are not implemented.
- Arithmetic checks, duplicate-invoice blocking, amount-based human-only approval,
  refusal of agent approval/payment attempts, and persistent audit records work.
  The blocked payment demonstration is a manual trigger and simulated, not a real
  transfer. Three-way matching against purchase orders and receipts is not built.
- Never claim actual payment, customer deployment, observed customer results,
  working OCR/PDF ingestion, or working three-way matching. EUR 473k belongs to an
  old synthetic calculation model and must not be used as a customer result.

### Atlas Partner

- Self-built prototype, not a mock-up and not a finished SaaS product. Root-page
  website analysis and ICP creation work. Some prospecting works but depends on an
  older LinkedIn-search vendor and has encountered usage limits; employee-count
  filtering exists only in the UI. The seven-stage pipeline works through a
  dropdown, not drag-and-drop. Delegated Cal.com booking can add a booking to the
  pipeline.
- Direct Google Calendar/Meet integration, complete inbound form capture, billing,
  self-service, and multi-customer operation do not exist. Do not call it a customer
  case study or a finished product.

## Scope boundaries

- Bareni currently declines high-sensitivity medical, legal, and financial work;
  bulk cold-email automation; scan-heavy OCR-dependent workflows; and requests
  that require unsupported compliance or security guarantees. Present these as
  current scope discipline, not claims that the work can never be automated.
- Do not say cold email is always illegal in Germany and do not give legal advice.
- Human approval is mandatory for money movement and other high-risk decisions.

## Voice, claims, numbers, and calls to action

- Sound like a technical expert using plain language: direct, calm, practical,
  founder-to-founder, and trustworthy. "The build stays technical; the conversation
  doesn't." Explain necessary jargon immediately.
- Trust outranks friendliness. At most one restrained dry-humour or understatement
  sentence per post. No memes, exclamation-mark bursts, hype, or jokes for their own
  sake.
- Never use revolutionary, 10x, game-changing, cutting-edge, unleash, supercharge,
  magic, or equivalent hype. Prefer concrete mechanisms and measured outcomes.
- Numbers require a source and status. Keep observed results, estimates, targets,
  synthetic data, and examples distinct. Never invent a benchmark, guarantee, ROI,
  saving, revenue lift, productivity result, or thesis-validated capability.
- Allowed: "we built" the three self-built demos/prototype; description of the
  actual features and disclosed limits; and description of Bareni as a consulting
  practice being built by the thesis author.
- Do not use a founder name, face, or career history as authority. Do not imply a
  multi-person team, legal registration, or current customer relationships.
- Standard primary CTA: "Book a free 30-minute diagnostic". Use it only for
  purchase-intent content, once, at the end. Informational posts use no CTA or one
  soft closing sentence. Demo CTA: "Watch the demo". At most one primary and one
  secondary CTA, only at the end. No popups, repeated CTAs, fabricated scarcity,
  countdowns, or pressure. A factual capacity statement such as "We take on a small
  number of pilots at a time" is allowed when relevant.

### 3.3 Actionability

output.title: The quiet cost of model deprecation
output.body:
If you are comparing automation with another hire, the quiet cost is not the first build. It is what happens when the model underneath it changes, gets retired, or becomes too awkward to keep using. Then the real question is whether you still want that workflow to exist at the same cost of upkeep.

For a small business, that shows up in ordinary places: customer-inquiry triage, lead qualification, or invoice handling. A workflow can look fine on day one and still need attention later if the model version shifts or the vendor changes pricing. That is not a disaster, but it is a maintenance decision, and it belongs in the business case from the start.

The practical next step is simple: before you approve any automation pilot, ask one blunt question: if the underlying model is upgraded, retired, or repriced, does the workflow keep working, or do we need to rebuild and pay again? If the answer is unclear, you do not have a finished plan yet; you have a hopeful sketch.

If you scope the ongoing model-version decision up front, you can compare automation against manual work honestly. That is usually where the hidden cost stops being quiet.

## Identity and audience

- The formal name is Bareni. Never write Baren-i.
- Bareni is a consulting practice being built by the author of the thesis. It is
  not yet a legally registered company. Marketing copy does not need to announce
  the absence of customers, but it must never imply invented customers, projects,
  testimonials, deployments, or results.
- Bareni is based in Frankfurt am Main and serves English-speaking customers
  globally. English is the only current consulting, delivery, and customer-data
  language. Germany is a location, not the current target market; do not present
  German customers or German-language delivery as current services.
- The intended reader is an owner-operator of a 1–10 person small business. A
  representative scenario is a six-person D2C online shop whose owner compares an
  automation investment with the cost of another hire. The representative pains
  are 8–10 hours a week of repeated customer questions, neglected sales leads,
  and manual invoice/data work. The 8–10 hours is a persona scenario, not a market
  statistic or observed customer result.
- The best-fit reader has tried ChatGPT but has not connected AI to a business
  workflow. Especially suitable businesses already work in English, use digital
  documents and SaaS tools, and have a frequent, repeatable workflow with a
  measurable outcome.

## Offer and delivery model

- Bareni is a one-person AI development and consulting practice that automates
  repetitive work for small businesses. Public voice uses "we".
- Services include a grounded knowledge assistant; controlled accounts-payable
  automation; Atlas Partner; general document, email, CRM, and back-office
  workflows using AI plus Zapier, Make, n8n, and small amounts of custom code;
  AI adoption consulting; and hands-on design, development, and deployment.
- Customer-facing language for the hands-on service should be simple: Bareni works
  inside the customer's environment and delivers a working system. "Forward
  Deployed Engineer" may be used in specialist discussion but is not the main
  customer-facing label.
- Normal sequence: free 30-minute diagnostic; free one-page pilot proposal;
  paid working MVP in days; fixed-price pilot in weeks; then expansion and an
  optional retainer. Do not insert a mandatory roadmap gate or separate "formal
  build" stage. Timings are intended scopes, not guarantees.
- The diagnostic identifies the one recurring workflow, says honestly whether AI
  fits, and—if it does—defines pilot scope, fixed price, and measures.
- Customers who want strategy only can buy the separate AI Strategy & Roadmap:
  a 90-day execution roadmap, success measures, build-versus-buy decision, and
  tool selection.
- Finished code is handed to the customer. Database, automation-tool, and API
  accounts are in the customer's name from the start. Retainer support is optional.
  Describe this as policy and no-lock-in positioning, not an absolute legal warranty.

  URL content; perform vector search and reranking; generate grounded LLM answers;
  and show sources. It works end to end locally, but the deployed public route is
  locked. Automated testing, rate limiting, and billing are planned, not working.
- RAG means retrieving relevant approved company documents before answering; in
  plain terms, the assistant looks in company material rather than the open web.
- Never imply production operation, customer validation, real customer documents,
  billing, rate limiting, or proven scale.

- Self-built demo using entirely synthetic data for a fictional German
  manufacturer. Text-based LLM invoice extraction was verified, while the default
  demo uses pre-extracted files. PDF/scan ingestion and OCR are not implemented.

  old synthetic calculation model and must not be used as a customer result.

- Self-built prototype, not a mock-up and not a finished SaaS product. Root-page
  website analysis and ICP creation work. Some prospecting works but depends on an
  older LinkedIn-search vendor and has encountered usage limits; employee-count
  filtering exists only in the UI. The seven-stage pipeline works through a
  dropdown, not drag-and-drop. Delegated Cal.com booking can add a booking to the
  pipeline.
- Direct Google Calendar/Meet integration, complete inbound form capture, billing,
  self-service, and multi-customer operation do not exist. Do not call it a customer
  case study or a finished product.

- Bareni currently declines high-sensitivity medical, legal, and financial work;
  bulk cold-email automation; scan-heavy OCR-dependent workflows; and requests
  that require unsupported compliance or security guarantees. Present these as
  current scope discipline, not claims that the work can never be automated.
- Do not say cold email is always illegal in Germany and do not give legal advice.
- Human approval is mandatory for money movement and other high-risk decisions.

  founder-to-founder, and trustworthy. "The build stays technical; the conversation

  synthetic data, and examples distinct. Never invent a benchmark, guarantee, ROI,
  saving, revenue lift, productivity result, or thesis-validated capability.
- Allowed: "we built" the three self-built demos/prototype; description of the

  practice being built by the thesis author.

  multi-person team, legal registration, or current customer relationships.

steps.instruction: Translate the abstract topic 'quiet cost of model deprecation' into one concrete, bounded workflow decision facing a small-business owner: the cost of rebuilding or retraining automated workflows when the LLM model powering them becomes unavailable, less capable, or pricing changes. Link this to the owner's decision context (hiring vs. automation investment) and the persona's constraint (human approval before money movement).

Illustrate the risk with a workflow example drawn from typical small-business automation (e.g., customer-inquiry triage, invoice extraction, or lead qualification). Use only self-built demo scope boundaries and no invented customer results. Show what happens when a model version is deprecated: the workflow breaks, retraining is required, and the owner must decide whether to fix it or revert to manual work.

Explain the business implication plainly: automation reduces repetitive labor cost only if the system remains stable. Model deprecation creates a hidden maintenance cost that must be weighed against the original investment. Use measured language and avoid invented numbers, benchmarks, or savings claims.

Name the owner's control: before committing to an automation investment, ask the vendor or builder whether the system will continue to work unchanged if the underlying model is upgraded, retired, or pricing changes. This is a diagnostic question, not a guarantee.

Provide a second practical next step: when evaluating automation vendors or proposing a pilot, include a clear definition of who owns the ongoing model-version decision and who bears the cost of retraining or switching if deprecation happens. Emphasize that human business authority approves any re-investment before money moves.

Close with a neutral, plain-language observation: automation is worth building when the workflow is stable and the maintenance burden is understood, not when the cheapest entry price hides future retraining costs. Do not include a CTA, booking invitation, or urgency. Use L01 to end with a practical diagnostic criterion the owner can apply immediately.
